messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Kiet Pham is a 51-year-old Vietnamese American policy analyst who lives with his wife in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. He presents following a wildfire that swept through his rural county approximately fourteen months ago, an event that has left a persistent mark on nearly every dimension of his daily functioning. His PCL-5 score of 55 places him firmly within the severe range, and the clinical picture that has emerged over the course of intake and early sessions is one of a man who once prided himself on careful, evidence-based thinking and who now finds that his own mind has become a source of profound distrust.

The fire came on a late August evening with almost no warning. Kiet and his wife had been monitoring reports throughout the day, but the wind shifted suddenly and the fire crested a ridge that emergency services had publicly designated as a natural containment line. Within forty minutes, evacuation orders reached their neighborhood. Kiet has described the next several hours in fragmented terms: the orange sky pressing down like a ceiling, the smell of smoke that was no longer distant but immediate and acrid, the way his chest tightened and his hands shook as he tried to load documents and medications into the car while his wife called out to him from the driveway. He lost track of time. He could not recall whether he had locked the door. He drove the wrong direction twice before finding the evacuation route. Their home survived, but three houses on their street did not, and Kiet spent six days in a community shelter before returning.

In the months that followed, the world began to feel constitutionally unreliable in ways it had not before. Kiet works primarily from home, drafting policy briefs and regulatory analyses, and the professional environment that once suited his methodical temperament has become a setting in which the symptoms find him with particular ease. He will be seated at his desk, deep in a document, when a neighbor lights a backyard fire or a nearby restaurant vents its kitchen, and the smell reaches him through an open window. What happens next is not, in his description, a simple startle — it is a full-body mobilization, a certainty that something has already gone wrong. He has begun keeping the windows closed even in summer, which his wife has noticed and which has become a source of quiet friction between them.

Kiet has also developed a vigilance around physical sensation that colors his days in a more diffuse way. When he feels even mildly unwell — a headache, a tight chest from poor posture, the mild nausea that sometimes accompanies long hours in front of a screen — he cannot dismiss it as ordinary. He had come to believe that his body's signals were the earliest warning system for something catastrophic, and so each twinge demanded attention and interpretation. He monitors himself throughout the workday in a way that makes sustained concentration increasingly difficult, and his output, once reliably strong, has slowed noticeably. His supervisor has commented on missed deadlines, which Kiet attributes to his difficulty concentrating but has not yet disclosed as connected to anything psychological.

What frightens him most, and what he returned to repeatedly in early sessions, is not the fire itself but his own responses since. He had always understood himself as someone who could assess risk accurately and act deliberately under pressure. The evacuation had shown him something different, and he had not been able to reconcile it. He was certain that the confusion, the intrusive sensory memories, the way any unscheduled or unpredictable event — a sudden change in plans, an unexpected phone call, a power flicker — could send his heart rate climbing, all pointed toward something fundamentally broken in him. He had begun to use the phrase "going crazy" in session not as hyperbole but as a genuine diagnostic hypothesis he was advancing about himself.

Kiet sought help after his wife found him sitting in the car in the garage at two in the morning, unable to explain why he had gone there. He told her he did not know what was happening to him. He came to the first appointment hoping, above everything, to be told that there was a name for this and that the name was not the one he feared.
